title: Breaking-change checks

story: Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, renames a field in the cloud's projects API from workgroup to workgroup_uid, because the ticket asked for clearer names. It is thorough. It changes the serializer, the frontend, every test, and also the Python SDK in fcp's sdk/ folder, so the SDK's own tests send the new name too. Everything inside the pull request agrees with everything else, and every check is green.

Customers do not run the sdk/ folder. They run rhino-health, the SDK package they installed from PyPI, the Python package index, months ago, and that version still sends workgroup. The day after the deploy their scripts fail with 400 Bad Request. The pull request had a reader it never tested: the code that was already released.
hook.question: How can CI test a pull request against the SDK version customers really have installed, before the change ships?

read.h: The reader that is not in the pull request
p: In the frontend, tsc protects you from a rename: every file that reads the old name is in the same repo, and it turns red. fcp's backend has readers outside the pull request. The breaking-change lesson met them: the on-prem client upgrades later than the cloud, old servers keep running during a deploy, and customers keep old versions of the SDK for months. A breaking change is one that such a reader cannot handle.

That lesson's checks compare descriptions: oasdiff compares the OpenAPI document of the branch with the one of the merge base, and buf compares the proto files. They are fast and catch most breaks. This lesson adds a check of a different kind for the most important outside reader, the SDK: run the code customers actually installed against the API of this commit, and see whether it still works. It catches what a description cannot, for example an SDK that relies on the order of a list, a default value, or a field the schema calls optional. A rule people call Hyrum's law says it well: with enough users, every behaviour you can observe will be depended on by somebody.

read.h: Install the release, not the folder
p: The trick is in how the test gets the SDK. The smoke test, a small set of tests that tries the most common calls and nothing more, imports the SDK with pytest.importorskip, and the SDK is not a dependency of the cloud project at all. CI installs one exact released version just for this run: it reads the latest version number from PyPI's JSON page for the package, then runs uv run --with rhino-health==<that version>, which adds the package to the environment for this one command only. Without --with, the test is skipped, so nobody runs it by accident against whatever happens to be installed.

Two details matter in fcp. The cloud project's pyproject.toml sets exclude-newer = "7 days", which tells uv to ignore packages published in the last week, and it applies to --with too, so the step must override it or yesterday's release would never be tested. And the latest release is not the only one in use: the SDK's owner picks the oldest version still supported, and the step tests that one as well. In the lab, a folder called released/ plays PyPI, and a wheel, the file format a Python package is published in, plays the release.
read.see:
$ uv run pytest -q tests
1 skipped in 0.04s
$ uv run --with released/projectsdk-1.0.0-py3-none-any.whl pytest -q tests/sdk_smoke
1 passed in 1.38s

read.h: A real server inside the test
p: The SDK speaks HTTP to a URL; it cannot use the in-process client from the earlier lessons. pytest-django has a fixture for exactly this, live_server: it starts this commit's Django on a free port in a thread of the test process, against the test database, and gives you its URL. The SDK then makes real requests, with real JSON, to the real code of the branch.

One rule comes with it. Normally each test runs inside a database transaction that is rolled back at the end, but the server thread has its own database connection and cannot see rows that the test has not committed. So the smoke tests use django_db(transaction=True): rows are really committed, and pytest-django empties the tables after each test instead of rolling back. That is slower, which is one more reason to keep the smoke test small: a few calls, the ones customers use most, chosen with the SDK's owner.

code.text:
"""The released SDK against this commit's API, over real HTTP. Run it with the released wheel:
uv run --with released/projectsdk-1.0.0-py3-none-any.whl pytest tests/sdk_smoke"""
import pytest

sdk = pytest.importorskip("projectsdk")  # not a dependency of the app on purpose: the test installs a release

pytestmark = pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True)  # the server thread must see committed rows


def test_the_released_sdk_creates_and_finds_a_project(live_server):
    client = sdk.Client(f"{live_server.url}/api")
    created = client.create_project("Lung CT", "lab-a")
    assert client.find_project("lung ct")["id"] == created["id"]

notes.text: Skipped unless a release was installed with --with. The app itself never depends on the SDK.
Committed rows, so the server thread can see what the test wrote.
live_server is this commit's Django on a free port. The SDK gets its URL like a customer gets ours.
The released code builds the request body, so a renamed field shows up here as a 400.

read.h: When the smoke test goes red
p: A red smoke test means the change would break customers who have not upgraded, so the change must be made in two steps instead. First expand: the API accepts both the old name and the new one, the SDK switches to the new name in its next release, and both versions keep working. Only when the oldest supported SDK no longer sends the old name do you contract, remove the old name, in a later pull request. The breaking-change lesson called this expand and contract; the smoke test is what proves the expand step really works for the old release.

The wrong reaction is to make the test agree with the change, for example by pointing it at the sdk/ folder of the branch instead of a release. The test then compares the pull request with itself and is green by definition. That is why the check's command lives in a CI file that agents may not change, and why a deliberate break, when one is ever needed, is a person's decision, recorded with the ticket key.

deeper.h: Go deeper: the other three checks in fcp's CI
p: oasdiff: a script exports the cloud's v2 OpenAPI document with drf-spectacular, without a database, for this commit and for a git worktree of the merge base, so even the first run has something to compare. oasdiff breaking --fail-on ERR fails the job on an error-level change, and a deliberate break is one line with the ticket key in a protected ignore file.

Migrations: django-migration-linter flags operations that break the old code still running during a deploy, such as dropping a column, and Squawk reads the SQL from manage.py sqlmigrate and warns about locks and table rewrites. Both start as advice for two weeks, then block. buf breaking checks the gRPC protos between the cloud and the on-prem client with the PACKAGE rule set, because the cloud calls the client's methods by name, so even a renamed method breaks old clients.

lab.title: Run the released SDK against your branch
needs: No Docker and no account: a local folder plays the package index
lab.goal: Build a small SDK release, smoke-test it against the API with live_server, watch the released version catch a rename that the repo's own SDK hides, then fix the API with an expand step.

guess.q: You rename workgroup to workgroup_uid in the API and in the repo's SDK folder. You run the smoke test twice: once with the SDK installed from the folder, once with the wheel released last month. What happens?

options.text: Both fail, because the API changed.
options.why: The folder's SDK was changed together with the API, so it agrees with it.

options.text: Both pass, because the field still holds the same value.
options.why: The released SDK still sends the old name, and the serializer now requires the new one.

options.text: The folder's SDK passes and the released one fails with 400, which is what customers would see.
options.why: Testing the folder compares the pull request with itself. Only the released code shows the break.

follow.say: Make the project: Django and DRF for the API, pytest and pytest-django for the tests.
follow.do: mkdir -p ~/academy-labs/g7-4 && cd ~/academy-labs/g7-4 && uv init --bare --python 3.13 && uv add "django>=5.2,<5.3" "djangorestframework>=3.17,<3.18" && uv add --dev pytest pytest-django && uv run django-admin startproject mysite . && uv run python manage.py startapp projects

follow.say: Write a small projects API that can also find a project by name, like the SDK needs.
follow.do:
printf '\nINSTALLED_APPS += ["rest_framework", "projects"]\n' >> mysite/settings.py
cat > projects/models.py <<'EOF'
from django.db import models


class Project(models.Model):
    name = models.CharField(max_length=120)
    workgroup = models.CharField(max_length=60)
EOF
cat > projects/views.py <<'EOF'
from rest_framework import serializers, viewsets

from .models import Project


class ProjectSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    class Meta:
        model = Project
        fields = ["id", "name", "workgroup"]


class ProjectViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):
    serializer_class = ProjectSerializer

    def get_queryset(self):
        name = self.request.query_params.get("name")
        return Project.objects.filter(name__iexact=name) if name else Project.objects.all()
EOF
cat > mysite/urls.py <<'EOF'
from rest_framework.routers import DefaultRouter

from projects.views import ProjectViewSet

router = DefaultRouter()
router.register("api/projects", ProjectViewSet, basename="project")
urlpatterns = router.urls
EOF
uv run python manage.py makemigrations projects

follow.say: Write the SDK as its own package, version 1.0.0, and build it into released/, which plays the package index.
follow.do:
mkdir -p sdk/src/projectsdk && cat > sdk/pyproject.toml <<'EOF'
[project]
name = "projectsdk"
version = "1.0.0"
requires-python = ">=3.13"
dependencies = ["requests>=2.32"]

[build-system]
requires = ["uv_build>=0.9,<0.13"]
build-backend = "uv_build"
EOF
cat > sdk/src/projectsdk/__init__.py <<'EOF'
"""The SDK customers install from the package index. Version 1.0.0 is in their scripts today."""
import requests


class Client:
    def __init__(self, api_url: str):
        self.api_url = api_url.rstrip("/")

    def create_project(self, name: str, workgroup: str) -> dict:
        response = requests.post(f"{self.api_url}/projects/", json={"name": name, "workgroup": workgroup}, timeout=30)
        response.raise_for_status()
        return response.json()

    def find_project(self, name: str) -> dict:
        response = requests.get(f"{self.api_url}/projects/", params={"name": name}, timeout=30)
        response.raise_for_status()
        return response.json()[0]
EOF
(cd sdk && uv build --out-dir ../released) && ls released

lab.build: Make the change safe with an expand step. In ProjectSerializer, add a to_internal_value(self, data) method: when the body has workgroup but no workgroup_uid, copy the value to workgroup_uid, then call super().to_internal_value(data). Release the SDK's 1.1.0 into released/ with (cd sdk && uv build --wheel --out-dir ../released). Then test every release in the folder with one loop: for wheel in released/*.whl; do echo "$wheel"; uv run --with "$wheel" pytest -q tests/sdk_smoke | tail -1; done. Both versions must pass.
checks: uv run pytest -q tests (without --with) still says 1 skipped.
released/ holds projectsdk-1.0.0 and projectsdk-1.1.0 wheels.
The loop prints 1 passed for both wheels.
A project created by SDK 1.0 shows workgroup_uid in the API's answer: the old name is accepted, the new name is what the API returns.
You did not change the smoke test or the released wheels to get there.
lab.fix: A teammate is tired of the red smoke test and changes the CI command from uv run --with released/projectsdk-1.0.0-py3-none-any.whl ... to uv run --with ./sdk ..., "because the released SDK is old anyway". Undo your expand step (go back to the renamed views.py) and run both commands. The new one is green. Explain why it can never be red for a field rename, and what the command must install instead.
explain: Why does the smoke test install a released version instead of using the SDK in the repo?
Why does the test need live_server and transaction=True, when the other API tests use an in-process client?
The smoke test is red after a rename. What are the two steps that make the change safe, and when does the second one happen?
lab.done: Both releases pass against your expanded API, and you can explain why a smoke test against the repo's own SDK proves nothing about customers.

check.q: Nova changed the API and the SDK folder together, and the SDK's own tests pass. Why is that not enough?

options.text: Customers run a released SDK version, which was not changed, so only a test with the release shows whether they break.
options.why: The folder and the API come from the same pull request, so they always agree. The release is the reader outside it.

options.text: Because the SDK's tests do not run in CI.
options.why: Even if they run, they test the changed folder, not what customers installed.

options.text: Because the SDK folder is written in a different language.
options.why: Both are Python. The problem is which version of the code runs, not the language.

check.q: Why does the smoke test use pytest.importorskip instead of listing the SDK as a dependency of the cloud project?

options.text: Because importorskip is faster than a normal import.
options.why: Speed is not the point; the point is which SDK version gets tested.

options.text: So CI decides exactly which release to install with --with for each run, and nothing tests a random installed version by accident.
options.why: Without --with the test skips; with it, it runs against exactly the version CI chose, such as the latest and the oldest supported.

options.text: Because pytest cannot import packages from PyPI.
options.why: It imports whatever is installed. --with is how the right version gets installed for one command.

check.q: The smoke test goes red after a field rename. What is the right fix?

options.text: Point the smoke test at the repo's SDK folder, which already has the new name.
options.why: Then the test compares the pull request with itself and can never fail on a rename.

options.text: Release a new SDK at once and ask customers to upgrade.
options.why: Customers upgrade when they choose. Until then their scripts break.

options.text: Expand first: accept both names in the API and release the SDK with the new name; remove the old name later, when no supported SDK sends it.
options.why: Old and new releases both keep working, and the smoke test proves it for the old one.

p: tests_api/sdk_smoke/test_published_sdk.py logs in with the latest rhino-health release through pytest-django's live_server, creates a project and finds it by name, against a site made by builder.site(). The API Tests job reads the version from https://pypi.org/pypi/rhino-health/json and runs uv run --group api-tests --with rhino-health==$SDK_VERSION pytest tests_api/sdk_smoke -m sdk_smoke, overriding the project's exclude-newer = "7 days" for this step; the SDK owner picks the oldest supported version to test too. While there, sdk-ci.yml sets TEST_USERNAME from SDK_TEST_PASSWORD and TEST_PASSWORD from SDK_TEST_USERNAME, which looks swapped and needs the owner's confirmation.

Three more checks join cloud CI. An OpenAPI breaking changes job exports the v2 schema with export_openapi.py for this commit and a worktree of the merge base and runs oasdiff with --fail-on ERR and the protected openapi-breaking-ignore.txt. The test job lints migrations added since main with django-migration-linter and Squawk, advisory for two weeks (known gap: --git-commit-id needs --project-root-path to see rhinoCore). The lint job runs buf breaking on common/ with PACKAGE rules (a removed field should be reserved, and deleting a reserved one still needs a person). Each check gets one line in Nova's checking guide.

tickets.why: The smoke test of the published SDK against this commit's API: this lesson.
oasdiff on the OpenAPI document of the merge base and the branch.
django-migration-linter and Squawk on new migrations.
buf breaking on the cloud-client gRPC protos.

words.plain: The SDK version on PyPI that customers installed; it can be months older than the repo's sdk/ folder.
A small test of the most common calls, to see quickly whether anything is badly broken.
Adds a package, such as an exact SDK release, to the environment for one command only.
A pytest-django fixture that runs the app on a free port inside the test, so real HTTP clients can call it.
Change a contract in two steps: first accept old and new, later remove the old when nobody uses it.

review.q: Write the CI command that runs the smoke test against one exact SDK release, and say what happens without --with.
review.a: uv run --with rhino-health==<version> pytest tests_api/sdk_smoke (plus the api-tests group in fcp). Without --with, importorskip skips the test.

review.q: Name three readers of fcp's backend that are not in a pull request, and the check that protects each one.
review.a: The published SDK (smoke test, oasdiff), the on-prem client (buf breaking), the old code during a deploy (migration linter and Squawk).

review.q: Why must the smoke test's command be on a protected path?
review.a: Because changing what it installs, for example to the repo's own folder, makes it always green. Agents may not change the checks they are judged by.

remember: Test the SDK customers really installed against your branch, and when it breaks, expand first and contract later.
